## Research Question

How does wildlife trade behave in online marketplaces — and what happens to demand when regulation intervenes?

## Background

Online marketplaces leave long, fine-grained records of wildlife trade that traditional monitoring misses. With collaborators at the National Institute for Environmental Studies and beyond, this project line uses those records to evaluate conservation policy: trade bans can push demand into unregulated threatened species ([Kubo et al. 2025, Conservation Letters](../../publications/items/2025-wildlife-trade-ban-spillover.qmd)), wildlife disease outbreaks reshape sales of management items ([Endo et al. 2025, One Health](../../publications/items/2025-wildlife-disease-online-sales.qmd)), and a decade of listings traces trade pressure on land hermit crabs ([Hsu et al. 2025, Global Ecology and Conservation](../../publications/items/2025-hermit-crab-online-trade.qmd)).

## Approach

Long-term marketplace datasets (millions of transactions across hundreds of species), causal inference around regulatory events, and text processing to identify species and trade context from the titles of traded items.

## Representative Findings

Regulation is not free: banning trade in listed species measurably boosted trade in unregulated, threatened alternatives — an early-warning problem this project aims to make assessable before rules take effect.
